# Independent audit: primitive extrusion and a shared shadow center

Sources:

- `candidate 372cc3158e8582ae`, Sections 1–7.
- `candidate 206ce63695a66fe5`, Sections 1–6.

Result: **PASS**, with the scope qualifications stated in the sources. These are exact mixed d-volume statements and ordinary quotient statements; they do not supply an intrinsic q<d extension or a general OC proof.

## 1. Exact arithmetic extrusion

A nonempty real interval [a,b] has floor(b)-ceil(a)+1 integer points; that expression is nonnegative, including an unsampled interval. Extending its upper endpoint by an integer k adds exactly k points. Tonelli over integer quotient bases and continuous coordinates proves the mixed-measure identity, including zero-volume fibers and d=0. Primitive-coordinate changes are unimodular and leave all continuous fiber measures unchanged.

The endpoint roof maps are Borel: the upper endpoint of a compact convex line section is upper semicontinuous on its compact projection. For each line, the newly sampled points are precisely floor(b)+r, 1<=r<=k. Thus the pushforward decomposition is exact, not merely a total-mass identity. Its halfspace indicator includes the actual floor term and every closed-boundary equality.

The continuous coefficient calculation frees precisely the primitive integer coordinate, so its length is lattice-normalized. The note correctly distinguishes that length from Euclidean length along a general primitive vector.

## 2. Full block and tails

The left, full, and right level ranges follow from the exact section condition a(x)<=t and b(x)>=t-k. Integer endpoint cases have the indicated ceil/floor conventions. The favorable halfspace traces contain the same quotient halfspace at the selected actual y; a vanishing quotient normal instead captures full favorable fibers. Accordingly the depth estimate handles oblique caps as well as pure integer caps.

Writing the two affine budgets as their mean minus Q times the distance to their crossing proves the exact finite optimization formula, even if its crossing lies outside the integer interval. The balanced-crossing lower estimate uses distance at most 1/2. The example with disjoint endpoint tails indeed has zero tail depth at the quotient center despite positive tail mass.

## 3. Unit-roof obstruction

The body under N sqrt(x) is convex. Its unit roof has the displayed half-open fibers, and its closure only adds endpoints already covered by the weak inequalities in the tangent-cap calculation. The necessary index bound is (j-j_0-1)^2<=2j_0; at most 2sqrt(2N)+1 indices qualify. Multiplying by the maximal fiber length gives the stated bound. The isolated top point has a zero-mass containing cap. Thus the bound applies to every possible roof center, including closure points.

The products in continuous coordinates and binary integer coordinates preserve this upper bound by an actual finite isolating tilt. The quotient raw depth is exactly 1/2: one selected cube supplies that lower bound, and an isolating tilt gives the matching upper bound. No claim transfers that depth to the nonconvex roof measure.

## 4. Arithmetic zonotope polynomial and whole caps

All quotient lattices are saturated before a new projected vector's divisibility is taken. For an independent extension, the product of the two finite indices in the source is exactly the enlarged index. This proves the coefficient m(I) and shows why primitive vectors alone do not imply unimodular coefficients. Dependent projected vectors contribute no new rank term. The calibration with index two is correct.

For each fixed closed halfspace, choosing each segment's favorable sign gives an actual Minkowski-sum inclusion in the same halfspace. Applying the exact polynomial to that compact convex cap proves the whole-cap lower polynomial, including degenerate caps and d=0 boundary mass. A zero normal pairing permits the doubled segment. The oblique rectangle example attains the one-direction coefficient. These are measures of projections of the same actual cap, not independently selected projected caps.

## 5. Ordinary convex-function quantiles

Compact sublevel sets ensure continuity from above and quantile attainment. Brunn–Minkowski proves the convexity of the root quantile directly, including the r=0 minimum sublevel. A positive-mass minimum gives an initial constant quantile interval; it is not discarded. The standard quantile distribution identity followed by Jensen gives the exact Gamma_d mean-sublevel bound. The standard simplex and the sum of its coordinates attain equality.

The two endpoint functions of an actual convex body satisfy the required semicontinuity, convexity/concavity, and boundedness. Ordinary Jensen places (t_0,g) in the actual body whenever t_0 lies in the interval of endpoint means. The two signs of the integer coefficient reduce projected cap membership to the correct convex sublevel inequalities; zero integer coefficient is covered by an affine function. Thus a single point controls every closed ambient cap's ordinary shadow.

Lattice membership is asserted only when that mean interval contains an integer. The exact positive-fiber example with mean interval [3/20,17/20] verifies why no unconditional rounding is possible. In higher integer rank the counting-measure triangle counterexample disproves the analogous mixed mean-sublevel step.

## 6. Preserved deficit and necessary center relocation

At the shared original integer point, the whole extrusion cap inequality preserves exactly the original raw OC deficit: its new mass term and new target term cancel. It does not erase a deficit by increasing the integer extrusion length.

The explicit four-fiber example has old fibers of width 2epsilon and new fibers small/full/full/small. Its total measure, old-point containing cap measure, and resulting upper bound 2/51 are exact. At the new point (0,g), the own full cube gives 1/2 and the reflected containment of the small left fiber in the full right fiber gives 2epsilon. This works for every oblique cap; pure integer caps give at least that amount directly. The resulting 13/51 exceeds Gamma_d/2. Finite binary-base isolating tilts verify the stated all-n product extension. This establishes center relocation, not an OC counterexample.

## Verification

Ran `work/math-venv/bin/python supporting computation verify_primitive_extrusion_zonotope_roof_two_sided.py`: **PASS, 7,469 exact checks**. Ran `work/math-venv/bin/python supporting computation verify_shared_endpoint_shadow_and_center_relocation_two_sided.py`: **PASS, 12,805 exact checks**. The ordinary quantile and shadow proofs were checked directly, including minimum atoms and the integer-mean-interval condition.

## Additional audit: arithmetic discrepancy and certified rounding

The subsequent source `candidate d358c029b6047209`, Sections 1–4, also passes a direct proof audit. The base one-coordinate error is at most one per actual nonempty line interval, including a singleton. In the induction, making coordinate 1 continuous and then applying the hypothesis to the other coordinates yields exactly A_{1}+sum_{J nonempty subset {2,...,n}}(A_J+A_{J union {1}}), with every nonempty coefficient appearing once. Thus neither a quotient index nor an error term is missing.

For a displaced continuous cap, moving its boundary by delta_i in coordinate i changes each parallel line cutoff by delta_i whenever the corresponding normal coefficient is nonzero; a zero coefficient changes nothing. Fubini consequently bounds the actual cap loss by |delta_i| times the full continuous projection volume. Applying the discrepancy estimate to that projection proves its upper bound by sum_{I containing i} A_I. These operations control all oblique normals uniformly.

The rounded-point lower bound is proved before membership. If it is positive, strict separation from the compact convex body would produce a closed containing halfspace with zero mass, contradicting the bound. Thus the membership conclusion is valid and is not centroid-rounding without a mass estimate. The heavy-fiber alternative supplies an actual point independently. The criterion remains conditional on its explicit coefficient inequality and on positive full mixed d-volume; no intrinsic lower-dimensional extension or general OC claim is inferred.
